name: Joel
author: The book names its author as Joel son of Pethuel, and nothing more is known about him or his family. He was a prophet, someone who spoke messages from God to the people. He knew Jerusalem, its temple and its priests well, which suggests he lived in or near the city, and some think he may have had close links with temple worship.
audience: Joel spoke to the people of Judah and Jerusalem, including the priests who led worship at the temple and the elders who led the community. They had just been struck by a devastating swarm of locusts and a drought that stripped the fields, vineyards and orchards bare. Food was scarce, and even the grain and wine used in daily temple offerings had run out.
era: The date of Joel is unclear because the book names no king. Traditionally it has been placed early, around 800 BC, perhaps while the boy-king Joash ruled Judah under the guidance of priests. Many scholars today date it later, around 500–350 BC, after the Jews returned from exile in Babylon and rebuilt the temple, when Judah was a small province under Persian rule. Either way, Judah was a small land whose people lived mostly by farming and whose survival depended on rain and harvest, and locust swarms were a dreaded and familiar disaster.

notes.1:13: Priests offered grain and wine to God at the temple every morning and evening; the famine meant these daily offerings could no longer be made.
notes.2:1: At the start of this passage a trumpet is blown: the shofar, a ram's horn sounded from Zion, Jerusalem's temple hill, to raise an alarm or call people together.
notes.2:12: In this passage the people are called to a fast and a sacred assembly, a recognised public response to national disaster, and the priests are to stand between the temple porch and the altar to pray.
notes.3:1: Later in this passage the valley of Jehoshaphat is named. The name means "the LORD judges," and the place is not clearly located; later tradition linked it to the Kidron Valley beside Jerusalem.
